window: Friday 2026-10-02 close -> Saturday 2026-10-03 7:05 AM ET (weekend edition)
lede: Soft jobs cut October hike odds to 21% and the Nasdaq 100 closed at a record, yet the 10-year rose to 5.28%.
geo_headlines: THE JOBS REPORT CAME IN WEAK. September payrolls rose 29,000 against 90,000 expected, and July and August were revised down by a combined 60,000; July now shows a loss of 10,000 jobs (Reuters). Unemployment rose to 4.2% as 485,000 people joined the labor force. Average hourly earnings rose 0.1%, 3.0% from a year ago, below the 3.2% forecast (investingLive). **Payroll growth has averaged about 51,000 a month over the past three months.**

OCTOBER HIKE ODDS FELL TO 21%. FedWatch now puts an October 28 hike at 21.0%, from 29.9% on Thursday and about 70% a week ago; a December hike is 85.0% priced. Chicago Fed President Goolsbee called the labor market steady and inflation the more pressing problem. Vice Chair Jefferson and Governor Bowman said Thursday there was no urgency to act again (New York Times).

BUT LONG YIELDS ROSE ANYWAY. The 10-year traded near 5.17% right after the report, then sold off to close at 5.28% on Treasury's curve (+4bp, +11bp on the week); the 2-year closed at 4.83% (+5bp) and the 30-year at 5.63%. The 10-year TIPS yield rose 4bp to 2.92%. A weak jobs number was not enough to sustain a bond rally while inflation stays high.

THE NASDAQ 100 CLOSED AT A RECORD. The Nasdaq 100 rose 1.00% to 30,807.93, above its September 22 record on both the close and the intraday high; Nvidia rose 1.3%. The S&P 500 rose 0.73% to 7,722.72, 0.98% below its August 13 record, and the Dow gained 0.49%. For the week, the S&P fell 0.27%, the Nasdaq 100 rose 0.65% and the Dow fell 1.26%. VIX 15.31.

G7 TO RELEASE 100 MILLION BARRELS. G7 leaders agreed to release 100 million barrels of reserves over four months, with a large diesel release in the first 20 days (CNBC). Brent December settled at $102.25 (-6 cents) after trading below $100 intraday; WTI November settled at $91.11 (-1.9%). Gold fell 1.0% to $4,162.30.

IRAN SAYS IT IS PREPARING FOR A 'MAJOR ROUND OF FIGHTING'. A source in Tehran told The National on Saturday that Iran expects the war to resume, while saying diplomacy remains open; Iran has not answered the US counterproposal. The Wall Street Journal reports a third carrier and up to 10,000 more troops heading to the region, with Trump weighing renewed strikes after the midterm elections (via Reuters). Weekend headlines land before Sunday evening's futures open.

NEXT WEEK IS LIGHT UNTIL EARNINGS. ISM services Monday at 10:00; FOMC minutes Wednesday at 2:00 PM; jobless claims Thursday; Michigan sentiment Friday at 10:00. Constellation Brands reports Tuesday, PepsiCo Thursday and Delta Friday (CNBC calendar).
client_frame_short: The jobs report was soft: only 29,000 jobs were added in September and unemployment rose to 4.2%. That all but took an October Fed hike off the table, and the Nasdaq 100 closed at a record. **Even so, the 10-year Treasury yield finished the day higher, at 5.28%, because inflation, not jobs, is what the bond market is worried about.** For clients, a cooling job market and high yields are not a crisis; they are a chance to lock in income. Nothing here calls for portfolio changes, and the next real tests are the Fed minutes Wednesday and how oil trades when futures reopen Sunday evening.
client_frame:
If a client asks over the weekend, the story is that the economy is cooling, which is what the Fed wanted, and stocks liked it.

The jobs data: employers added only 29,000 jobs in September, and the two prior months were revised down by 60,000. Unemployment rose to 4.2%, partly because nearly half a million people started looking for work. Wage growth slowed to 3.0% a year. That is a softening labor market, not a collapse.

The Fed: markets now see about a 21% chance of an October rate hike, down from about 70% a week ago. Several Fed officials said this week they are in no hurry. Some investors still expect rates to stay "higher for longer" because inflation remains well above the Fed's 2% target (CNBC).

Stocks: the Nasdaq 100 closed at a record on Friday, led by chip companies after Micron's strong results. The S&P 500 is within 1% of its August record. Gains are still narrow, though: in September, the equal-weighted S&P 500 lagged the cap-weighted index by 4.6 percentage points, one of the widest gaps since 2003 (CNBC).

The puzzle clients may notice: long-term interest rates did not fall. The 10-year Treasury yield dipped right after the report, then closed higher at 5.28%. Long rates are being driven by inflation that is still running hot at home and abroad, large government borrowing, and oil near $100. The G7 agreed Friday to release 100 million barrels of reserves, which may help fuel prices, but Iran says it is preparing for more fighting.

For clients, the message holds: high-quality bonds now pay about 5% for a decade, an opportunity for income; equity plans built for the long run do not need changing because of one jobs report. What would change the view: a 10-year close above 5.40%, a 30-year above 5.75%, or a resumption of US strikes on Iran that sends Brent well above $105.
